title: Rahu's last years:
bumpy, then it turns.
summary: Why the end of Rahu's eighteen years is read as the bumpiest part, what each of the last three short visits is said to bring, and what changes when Jupiter's sixteen years begin.

basis: This guide is about the planetary periods in your birth chart, which are worked out from the Moon's exact position when you were born.

inside: How Rahu's eighteen years are divided, with a table of every sub-period and its length
What the last three visits, the Sun, the Moon and Mars, are each read to bring
Why the handover is read as unsettled, what Jupiter's years are said to bring, and what to do now
intro: If you are near the end of Rahu's period, you may feel it. The last stretch of this long chapter is often described as the bumpiest: restless, emotional, impatient, as if everything wants to happen at once. People in these years often say they feel close to something new and unable to reach it.

The tradition has a clear map of these years, and a clear end. This guide shows how Rahu's eighteen years are divided, what each of the last three short visits is read to bring, why the handover feels unsettled, and why what comes next is read as one of the calmest and most generous periods a chart can run.

sections.label: The chapters
title: Life in
nine chapters.
paragraphs: Vedic astrology divides a life into chapters called planetary periods, or dashas. There are nine, one for each of the planets the tradition counts, and together they last one hundred and twenty years. Which chapter you were born into depends on where the Moon was at your birth, so two people of the same age can be in very different chapters.

Rahu's chapter lasts eighteen years. Rahu is the hungry head of the dragon: a head with no body, always wanting, never full. In his years people are read as wanting more: a bigger city, a bigger job, a new life, something foreign or unusual. That appetite can carry you a long way, and it can also leave you restless.

sections.label: Inside the eighteen years
title: Nine visits
inside one chapter.
paragraphs: Every chapter is divided into nine sub-periods, one for each planet, in a fixed order that starts with the chapter's own planet. Each one lasts in proportion to that planet's own years. In Rahu's chapter the order and lengths are these. Find where you are, and you can see how far you are from the end.

rows.note: The opening: new appetite, new directions, often a sudden change of scene.
Read as one of the kinder stretches: teachers, study, growth that feels earned.
Hard work and pressure, read as building something solid if you keep going.
Trade, skills, writing and quick thinking; a busy, clever stretch.
A strange, inward stretch when the two halves of the dragon meet; letting go of something.
The longest sub-period: comfort, love, money and pleasure, with Rahu's appetite on top.
The first of the last three: pressure to prove yourself, clashes with authority, wanting to be seen.
Big feelings, home and family on your mind, moods that rise and fall quickly.
The very last: restless energy, impatience, wanting everything done now. Then Jupiter begins.

sections.label: The last three
title: The Sun, the Moon,
then Mars.
paragraphs: The final three and a half years of Rahu's chapter come in three short visits. They are short, and they are intense, because each one brings a strong personal planet into Rahu's restless story.

The Sun comes first, for about eleven months. The Sun stands for the self, authority and recognition, and the tradition reads its visit inside Rahu's years as pressure to prove yourself: wanting to be seen, clashing with people in charge, or feeling that your effort is not yet getting the credit it deserves.

The Moon comes next, for a year and a half. The Moon is the mind, home and mother, and its visit is read as a stretch of big feelings. Moods can rise and fall quickly, and family, home and the people who raised you are often on your mind.

Mars comes last, for about a year. Mars is energy, courage and drive, and inside Rahu's years it is read as restlessness and impatience: wanting everything done now, quick to snap, eager to start the next life before this one is finished. It is also read as a lot of energy to finish things with, if you point it somewhere useful.

sections.label: The handover
title: The last mile
of a long drive.
paragraphs: The tradition calls the meeting point of two chapters a junction, dasha sandhi in Sanskrit, and reads it as unsettled. One way of living is ending before the next has fully begun. It is a lot like the last mile of a long drive: you are tired, you can almost see where you are going, and every small delay feels bigger than it is.
Knowing this helps. A wobbly feeling in the last months of Rahu's chapter is not a sign that something has gone wrong. It is the shape of the handover.

sections.label: What comes next
title: Jupiter's sixteen years
of calmer growth.
paragraphs: After Rahu comes Jupiter, for sixteen years. Jupiter is pictured as a round, laughing teacher carrying a gift, and his chapter is read as one of the kindest in the whole cycle: learning, family, good advice, a growing sense of meaning, and growth that comes steadily rather than in sudden leaps.

Many people describe the start of Jupiter's chapter as breathing out after a long time holding their breath. What Rahu made you hungry for, Jupiter is read as helping you understand and build properly.

sections.label: Rahu in the sky now
title: Scorpio, Leo
and Pisces Moons.
paragraphs: Separately from the chapters, Rahu also moves through the sky, about a year and a half in each sign. On Saturday, December 5, 2026, he moves into Capricorn and stays there until June 23, 2028.

The tradition reads Rahu as doing best in three houses counted from your Moon sign: the third, the sixth and the eleventh, the houses of effort, of beating obstacles, and of gains. Capricorn is the third house for a Scorpio Moon, the sixth for a Leo Moon and the eleventh for a Pisces Moon. For those three Moon signs, these eighteen months are read as Rahu's hunger working for you, whatever chapter your own chart is running.

steps.name: Do not make your wildest leap in the last months
steps.text: The junction is read as a poor time for the most dramatic decision of the whole chapter. If a big move can wait until Jupiter's years have settled in, the tradition suggests letting it.

steps.name: Finish what you started
steps.text: Rahu's years open many doors. The last stretch is a good time to walk through the ones that matter and close the rest, so you start the next chapter lighter.

steps.name: Give Mars a job
steps.text: In the last year, the restless energy is read as useful when it has a target. Pick one thing to complete and pour the impatience into it.

steps.name: Look after your routines
steps.text: Steady sleep, steady meals and a little daily quiet are what people traditionally use to steady Rahu. They help most when everything feels urgent.

faq.q: How do I know if I am in Rahu's chapter?
faq.a: From your birth chart. Your chapters are worked out from the Moon's exact position when you were born, so you need your birth date, time and place. AstrolGuru shows your current period and sub-period straight away.

faq.q: Are the last years of Rahu always hard?
faq.a: No. The tradition reads them as bumpy and restless, not as bad. How they feel depends on the rest of your chart, and many people use the energy of these years to finish things they have worked on for a long time.

faq.q: Does Jupiter's period start well for everyone?
faq.a: It is read as one of the kindest chapters, but how it plays out depends on where Jupiter sits in your own chart. The handover itself is read as unsettled for everyone, then easing as the new chapter settles in.

note: Period lengths follow the classical Vimshottari scheme of 120 years. Rahu's position is calculated with the Lahiri ayanamsa; dates are US Eastern time.
